newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries up a bit at open, T-note sale ahead.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries up a bit at open, T-note sale ahead.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened barely higher on Wednesday as the market focused again on fresh supply.
The Treasury will sell $12.5 billion in five-year notes in the afternoon. The deadline for bids is 1300 EDT/1700 GMT. Auction results are due around 1340 EDT.
On Tuesday, the Treasury sold $18.25 billion in two-year notes. The auction went well but despite that, there was little follow-through buying, analysts said.
The session is devoid of fresh economic data to guide it so analysts expect the market to remain rangebound.

The market gets jobless claims data on Thursday and September durable goods orders on Friday but even these reports are expected to be less influential than next week's raft of data, which include the employment cost index, third-quarter GDP (gross domestic product), the NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Managers) index and the crucial monthly (October, this time) payroll employment report.

MMS analysts said the market's better tone this morning was due to "bargain hunting in Japan (helped by the softer dollar), some central bank buying, and from a swap bid on the ABN Amro $500 million five-year offering."

As for the five-year note sale, "the question is whether there is enough demand beyond the short and arbitrage bidding," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "That's what is going to make or break the auction."
Stiles said after the sale is completed, "the market will probably be a little heavy but will try to do better" ahead of the durable goods orders report on Friday.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that durable goods orders rose two percent in September after falling 3.2 percent in August.
"Durables are expected to show a solid rebound from a very weak August," said Stiles. "Therefore, it's expected to be neutral for the market."

In when-issued trade, the five-year notes to be sold today were yielding 6.3175 percent. Five-year Treasury notes last were auctioned on September 26. At that time the notes were sold at a 6.409 percent yield, the bid-to-cover ratio was 2.57, and non-competitive bids totaled $477 million.
William McDonough, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, will speak at a small business awards luncheon in New Jersey at 1300 eDT/1700 GMT.
"We're going to haave McDonough today but he has already made his point earlier this week about the Employment Cost Index and wage pressures being important," said Stiles.

Analysts said the market would watch the dollar. The dollar weakened on Tuesday after a wire service reported that an unnamed White House official predicted that the U.S. Japan trade gap would begin to widen after months of shrinkage.

"The concern is that perhaps the Administraiton is going to start to become concerned about the deterioriation in the trade balance and perhaps try to talk the dollar down," said Stiles. "Since the dollar rally has correalated well with the bond recovery over the last month, people would worry about the bond market if it suddenly looked like the dollar was topping out and was going to weaken."
In early trade, three-month, six-month, and year bill rates were all unchanged at 4.99 percent, 5.14 percent and 5.27 percent, respectively.
The 6-1/2 percent ten-year note was unchanged at 99-15/32, yielding 6.57 percent.
After being up 2/32 its initial trades, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond erased the small gain and was off 1/32 to 98-20/32, yielding 6.86 percent, in early activity.
